title: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I strongly suspect that the vast majority of physical laws discovered so far are not truly fundamental, but are instead merely emergent features of the large-scale behavior of some ultimate underlying rule.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 9, “Fundamental Physics”; section “Ultimate Models for the Universe” (from p. 465), p. 470. Scope: known laws of physics

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch09-11: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.23

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Particular effective theories can be shown to emerge from deeper models, but the vast-majority statement about all known laws cannot be tested independently of a chosen ontology. Existing observations underdetermine which level is fundamental.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The claim would require an agreed criterion separating fundamental from emergent laws and knowledge of the ultimate rule; neither is supplied, so cataloging current laws cannot yield a decisive result.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The simplicity comparison has no fixed coding language.

Fundamental versus emergent is model-dependent.

The ultimate underlying rule is unknown.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many familiar laws, including continuum thermodynamics and fluid mechanics, already have published derivations from more microscopic models, so that part of the claim can be checked. Particle data show other regularities still put in by hand. Without a census of laws and without the ultimate rule, 'the vast majority' and the claim that their simplicity says little about that rule stay only partly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify published physical laws by whether they are derived as large-scale limits of a more microscopic theory or are inputs with no such derivation, then ask whether the simple derived laws constrain the microscopic rule. A census in which most textbook laws are effective theories supports the claim; a finding that most laws are irreducible inputs would refute the 'vast majority'.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Truly fundamental' is defined only relative to an unknown ultimate rule.

There is no canonical list of 'physical laws discovered so far' on which to compute a majority.
